newsitem.title: USA: U.S. bankruptcy court judge raps Sears.
newsitem.headline: U.S. bankruptcy court judge raps Sears.

text.p: A U.S. bankruptcy court judge lashed out at Sears, Roebuck and Co. in a case which has become the focus of a credit card scheme which could cost the retailer tens of millions of dollars.

Sears, as a matter of company policy, misled many of its bankrupt credit card holders to believe they had to repay their debts to the company, even though those bills had been nullified by a bankruptcy court, U.S. Bankruptcy Court Judge Carol Kenner wrote in a court brief.
"Sears preyed on the debtor when he was financially most vulnerable and powerless; and in doing so it deprived him of the fresh start that Congress intended he should have," she said.
Between January 1995 and January 1997, the nation's second largest retailer used the tactic on more than 2,700 of its credit card holders in Massachusetts alone, the judge said.
The company earlier this month admitted that it exercised "flawed legal judgment" and would refund tens of millions of dollars it collected from bankrupt credit card holders around the country.

Sears said from 1992 through February 1997, it reached about $400 million in so-called reaffirmation agreements with card holders around the country, and was conducting a nationwide audit of the agreements. Any improperly handled agreements would be refunded, Sears said.
Sears had previously trumpeted to financial analysts its ability to reach such payment agreements, called reaffirmations, with bankrupt holders of its credit cards.
Reaffirmations are required to be submitted to bankruptcy courts, but Sears routinely failed to file the agreements and thus flouted the laws for its own benefit, Kenner said.
"Sears here made a conscious decision to disregard the clear requirements of the law because it was more expeditious and profitable to do so," Kenner wrote.

In the particular case Kenner ruled on, Francis Latanowich, whose monthly income was a $500 disability payment, agreed to pay Sears $28 a month on his credit card debt of $1,161 even though his debt had been discharged by a bankruptcy court.
Sears threatened to repossess a TV and other goods he bought unless he agreed to the reaffirmation, and then failed to submit the agreement to a bankruptcy court, Kenner wrote.
The judge ordered Sears to pay compensatory damages of $239.06, but reserved judgment until a later date on punitive damages, which could be much higher.

Kenner said earlier this month she was prepared to order Sears to pay punitive damages of $500 for each of the more than 2,700 credit card holders in Massachusetts alone for a total of more than $1.36 million.

"In the form of punitive damages, the court will supply this incentive by making it significantly more costly for Sears to do business by illegal methods than by legal ones," Kenner wrote in her Wednesday decision.
Officials with Sears did not return phone calls seeking comment.
